title: Ja'far the flyer
hook: killed at Mu'tah holding the banner, told he had two wings in the garden (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umm Ayman, who wept because revelation had stopped. Your line was my mother after my mother.

In Medina, Abdullah ibn Umar meets a man in the street and greets him with a strange name. Peace be upon you, he says, son of the one with two wings. He is the son of Ja'far, the Prophet's cousin, and his father is dead. Every time Ibn Umar met him, Bukhari says, he greeted him that way. Not son of the martyr. Not son of the brave. Son of the one with two wings. To understand it, you have to go to a battlefield, and a banner passing from one hand to the next. Today: Ja'far.
screen: `A GREETING IN THE STREET.` → `SON OF THE ONE WITH TWO WINGS.` → `BACK TO A BATTLEFIELD.`

segments.voice: Ja'far ibn Abi Talib was Ali's brother and a cousin of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Years before, tradition says, he had led the believers who took refuge in Abyssinia and spoke for them before its Christian king. Now an army is sent north, to a place called Mu'tah. Bukhari records how the Prophet set the command: Zayd ibn Harithah leads. If Zayd is killed, Ja'far. If Ja'far is killed, Abdullah ibn Rawahah. Three names, in order, each ready to take what the one before let fall. Then, in Medina, before any messenger had come back, the Prophet stood and gave the news, with tears in his eyes, Bukhari says. Zayd took the banner and was killed. Then Ja'far took it and was killed. Then Ibn Rawahah took it and was killed. And then, he said, one of the swords of God took it, and God gave them victory. Tradition adds the detail people remember: Ja'far held the banner in his right hand until it was cut, then in his left, then held it to his chest with what was left of his arms. That part comes from the biographies. What the hadith collections keep is the answer. A report in Tirmidhi has the Prophet saying he saw Ja'far flying in the garden with the angels. So Ibn Umar greets the son as son of the two-winged one. The arms he lost holding the banner, tradition says, were given back as wings. Two wings.
screen: `THE PROPHET'S COUSIN.` · `ZAYD, THEN JA'FAR, THEN IBN RAWAHAH.` · `THE BANNER PASSES HAND TO HAND.` · `FLYING IN THE GARDEN.` · then, large: `TWO WINGS.`

segments.voice: Think of the things you carry for other people, a child's ride to school, a parent's medicine, a promise at work, a prayer you keep, and choose one that has started to slip. Picture taking it up again in your right hand and keeping hold of it through one ordinary, tiring day; not every duty, just this one. If you pray, you can ask for steadiness to carry it.
Ja'far, who took the banner at Mu'tah after Zayd fell, was killed holding it, and whom the tradition calls the one with two wings. Today's word.
Your line: two wings. Each of the three held the banner to the end. That's day eight hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims call Ja'far ibn Abi Talib al-Tayyar, the flyer, and Dhul-Janahayn, the one with two wings, and retell the account of Mu'tah from Sahih al-Bukhari.

chat.meaning: In Tirmidhi the Prophet says he saw Ja'far flying in the garden with the angels; tradition says the arms he lost were given back as wings.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4261 (the order of command at Mu'tah: Zayd, then Ja'far, then Abdullah ibn Rawahah)

notes: The index hook says 'told he had two wings in the garden (Bukhari)'. Bukhari 3709 has Ibn Umar's greeting; the vision of Ja'far flying is from Tirmidhi 3763. Attributed accordingly. Confirm numbers.
The banner held in the right hand, then the left, then to the chest is from the sira; framed as such. No count of wounds given.
Ja'far leading the refugees and speaking before the Negus is framed as 'tradition says'.
'One of the swords of God' refers to Khalid ibn al-Walid; not named, to keep the focus. 'God gave them victory' paraphrases Bukhari 4262; confirm.
Bukhari 3709 says Ibn Umar greeted him this way whenever he met him; the hook says 'every time'. Confirm.
Original: confirm vocalization of Dhul-Janahayn and stress.
Editor: hook no longer calls Ja'far's son 'a young boy' (Bukhari 3709 gives no age); cut the narrator's instruction at the end of the teach.
